items.title: A Finnish Metal Detectorist Was Shocked to Unearth a Trove of Viking Age Silver in His Hometown. Then His Detector Went Off Again
items.summary:
A Finnish Metal Detectorist Was Shocked to Unearth a Trove of Viking Age Silver in His Hometown. Then His Detector Went Off Again

Weighing a combined ten
items.text:
A Finnish Metal Detectorist Was Shocked to Unearth a Trove of Viking Age Silver in His Hometown. Then His Detector Went Off Again

Weighing a combined ten pounds, the artifacts are estimated to be 1,000 years old and constitute Finland’s largest coin hoard of the era

A metal detectorist in southern Finland has unearthed the country’s largest hoard of Late Iron Age silver coins to date. Buried in the 11th century in what’s now the town of Sysmä, the ten-pound collection contains remnants of jewelry and likely thousands of coins.

The detectorist, Kalle Lappinen, was scanning ground in his hometown last week when his metal detector signaled. He began digging, and then his handheld probe “roared,” Lappinen tells the New York Times’ Ephrat Livni.

“With the fury of a monkey, I dug through the soil, bottom moraine and cobblestones,” he recalls. He found “a pile of coins” about 18 inches down and, once he had “recovered from the adrenaline rush,” reported it to authorities. Then, not far away, Lappinen’s metal detector signaled again, prompting him to dig a second hole—and find yet another trove of coins.

Did you know? The Staffordshire Hoard

One of the most famous discoveries by a metal detectorist was made in 2009, when Terry Herbert unearthed an astonishing

cache of some 3,500 pieces of early medieval gold and silver metalwork in Staffordshire, England, that were eventually valued at more than $5 million.

The next day, Esko Tikkala, an archaeologist at the nearby Lahti City Museums, arrived to inspect and excavate the artifacts. According to a statement from the museums, the collection includes a fragment of hacksilver, a silver bracelet, a silver charm, a silver bead and many silver coins—which have not yet been cleaned, separated or counted. The coins alone weigh just under ten pounds; experts say there must be thousands.

“There are quite a lot of coins in this hoard,” and they await detailed analysis, Tikkala tells Live Science’s Tom Metcalfe. “There will definitely be scientific articles published on the hoard as a whole, as well as more detailed studies of the coins themselves.”

The hoard likely dates to between about 1000 and 1050 C.E., Tikkala says. This half-century corresponds with the tail end of the Viking Age, which historians typically confine to about 793 C.E.—when Vikings raided Lindisfarne in Britain—through 1066, the date of the Norman Conquest. Lahti City Museums have thus classified the hoard as a “Viking Age” find.

“The term ‘Viking Age’ does not imply that there were Vikings in Finland,” Tikkala explains. “We have no sources suggesting that Finland was ‘Viking’ in the same sense as regions of present-day Sweden, Norway and Denmark.”

Though Finland isn’t Scandinavian and wasn’t Viking territory, by the 11th century, some Swedes had settled on its southern coasts. As Toni Paukku, an archaeologist at the Lahti Museums, tells the Times, “Finland was strongly connected to the Scandinavian cultural sphere, boosted by the trade of Scandinavian seafarers—some of whom were indeed Vikings—across the Baltic Sea.”

The silver hoard found by Lappinen was buried in two birch-bark containers, about 40 feet apart, per the statement. Experts don’t know why it was buried, but historians do know that the close of the Viking Age was an unstable period in Finland, as Swedes and Danes raided its regions where Finns, Russians and Germans traded.

“Intentionally hidden treasures like these are somewhat common for this era in Finland,” Paukku tells the Times, citing societal unrest due to external threats. “One can only say that whoever they”—the people who hid the silver—“were, they did not come back to collect the treasure. … No burials appear to be associated with the hoard.”

Lappinen’s find marks the latest in a remarkable tally of silver discoveries this year. Just over a week ago, a Dane landscaping in his backyard accidentally unearthed Denmark’s largest hoard of Viking silver, and in April, metal detectorists in Norway found their country’s largest deposit of Viking silver. The Sysmä collection has easily taken the title of Finland’s largest silver coin hoard, which previously belonged to a five-pound stash unearthed near the southern coast in 1895.

The Sysmä discovery is “a case of responsible and responsive detecting, which has produced a promising archaeological discovery,” Eljas Oksanen, an archaeologist at the University of Helsinki, tells the Times. It shows that “detectorists can produce a considerable amount of new valuable information about the past, not the least because they (as in this case) search in areas that professional archaeologists do not go to.”

items.title: Did You Suffer a Sweltering August? You Weren't Alone. It Tied for the Month With the Hottest Global Temperatures on Record
items.summary:
Did You Suffer a Sweltering August? You Weren’t Alone. It Tied for the Month With the Hottest Global Temperatures on Record

Last month, the air temperature
items.text:
Did You Suffer a Sweltering August? You Weren’t Alone. It Tied for the Month With the Hottest Global Temperatures on Record

Last month, the air temperature averaged 62.53 degrees Fahrenheit, tying with July 2023 as the toastiest month ever documented by the European Union’s climate service

Sara Hashemi
| Daily Correspondent

September 11, 2026 12:57 p.m.

If you thought this August was especially hot, you aren’t wrong. According to the European Union’s Copernicus Climate Change Service, last month tied with July 2023 as the hottest month on its record, which dates back to 1940.

The global surface air temperature averaged 62.53 degrees Fahrenheit in August. That’s almost 3 degrees above pre-industrial levels, which exceeds the 2.7-degree threshold set by the Paris Agreement, an international treaty on climate change adopted by nearly 200 nations in 2015.

“These observations show how climate change is driving extremes across both the atmosphere and the oceans,” says Samantha Burgess, a climate scientist and deputy director of Copernicus, in the statement. “The impacts of these conditions are increasingly being felt by communities, economies and ecosystems across the world.”

Western Europe had its hottest summer ever as it dealt with back-to-back heatwaves that led to at least 35,000 deaths. So did the contiguous United States, where the average temperature in August hit 75.6 degrees—3.5 degrees above the 20th-century average. It was the warmest season on the U.S.’s record, which stretches back to 1895, according to the National Centers for Environmental Information. July was even hotter, averaging 76.9 degrees and breaking the infamous Dust Bowl record set in July 1936, per Jeff Masters and Bob Henson at Yale Climate Connections.

Other parts of the world were also drier than average, including northern Mexico, parts of Canada, the Maghreb, part of the Horn of Africa, Siberia and large parts of Asia, China, South America, South Africa and northern Australia, according to Copernicus. And at 69.9 degrees, the average sea surface temperature outside the polar regions was the highest on record for any August, passing the record previously set for the month in 2023.

According to Copernicus, the record-breaking summer heat likely arose from two factors: a strengthening El Niño in the Pacific Ocean and global heating from human use of fossil fuels. Scientists note that the naturally occurring climate pattern of El Niño alone is not responsible for these temperatures.

“While El Niño is starting to ramp up the heat, the underlying driver remains our relentless burning of fossil fuels. Climate change makes every El Niño hotter, and until we stop burning coal, oil and gas these record-shattering months will simply keep on coming,” says Friederike Otto, a climate scientist at Imperial College London, to Seth Borenstein at the Associated Press.

Quick fact: El Niño events have been growing stronger

Using records captured in corals, a study published in August found that although El Niño climate swings occur naturally, they’ve become stronger in recent decades. That’s probably happening because humans have been heating up the planet.

The Copernicus finding follows a United Nations report that warned that passing the Paris Agreement’s 2.7-degree threshold is probably unavoidable. According to the U.N. document, titled “Limiting Overshoot” and published on September 2, the world now needs to focus on minimizing peak warming and finding ways to bring temperatures back down.

Simon Stiell, the executive secretary of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, writes on social media that the Copernicus report is “another stark warning sign from our heating planet,” and underscores the need for humans to stop burning coal, oil and gas. “This is the spiraling price of humanity’s fossil fuel addiction, and the global climate crisis it is fueling.”

Clair Barnes, an extreme weather researcher at Imperial College London, echoes that sentiment. “Until we stop burning fossil fuels, these records will continue to tumble, and the extremes will worsen faster than we are able to adapt,” she tells Matt McGrath at the BBC News. “Crucially, how much worse we allow it to get remains within our hands.”

Sara Hashemi
| Daily Correspondent
September 11, 2026 12:57 p.m.

If you thought this August was especially hot, you aren’t wrong. According to the European Union’s Copernicus Climate Change Service, last month tied with July 2023 as the hottest month on its record, which dates back to 1940.

The global surface air temperature averaged 62.53 degrees Fahrenheit in August. That’s almost 3 degrees above pre-industrial levels, which exceeds the 2.7-degree threshold set by the Paris Agreement, an international treaty on climate change adopted by nearly 200 nations in 2015.

“These observations show how climate change is driving extremes across both the atmosphere and the oceans,” says Samantha Burgess, a climate scientist and deputy director of Copernicus, in the statement. “The impacts of these conditions are increasingly being felt by communities, economies and ecosystems across the world.”

items.author: Vicky
items.summary: Bill Gurley spent years on Wall Street, built his career as a partner at Benchmark, worked through Uber’s hypergrowth era, and now serves on the board of the
items.text:
Bill Gurley spent years on Wall Street, built his career as a partner at Benchmark, worked through Uber’s hypergrowth era, and now serves on the board of the Santa Fe Institute, where he studies complexity and systems thinking.

Featured clips

Obsessive Learning in Founders

The Craft of Storytelling and Writing

Available Now: YouTube | Spotify | Apple Podcasts | Transcript | X

In this episode, Bill shares the mental models he returns to most often, including systems thinking, second- and third-order effects, and the importance of understanding both the bedrock of your field and the bleeding edge.

He explains what separates great founders, why storytelling and product instincts matter, how he uses AI across different models, and what he sees coming in open source, China, stablecoins, tokenization, payments, and venture capital.

+ Check out Runnin’ Down a Dream: How to Thrive in a Career You Actually Love

++ Check out the Granola Notes

Tiny Lessons

Trajectory matters more than the starting place.

“Success requires balancing a deep knowledge of history with an obsessive focus on the technological edge where disruption happens.”

“I think more people would benefit by studying the history of whatever field they’re in.”

“If it’s tedious to learn, it isn’t a passion. I don’t think you’re in the right lane.”

“I think that anybody in any field should want to be curious about the bleeding edge and what happens.”

“You should understand the really old stuff, the history, because it’s differentiating and shows a passion and it gives you a great frame of mind, but you also want to really understand the new edge. If you do both of those things, I think you’re a power player in your field.”

“If you have to write it out and make it stand alone and be cogent, you’ll think through more of the problems and it’ll be more cohesive and you’ll figure out the loose ends and you’ll tie them up.”

“If regulation gets extremely difficult and mundane and expensive, that could actually lead to more oligopoly.”

“I would describe complex systems as multivariable nonlinear systems. And multivariable nonlinear systems are very hard to predict. They can behave one way for a long time, and then one variable can switch and they can behave another way—the weather, stock markets, all these things. There are consequences that can be first, second, or third-order. You can’t just think with a linear model or just think about one variable because things can go way off the path. You need to be aware that if you make a change here, it could change something here, which could change something there, and it has to be the whole system.”

“You’ve got to be really conscious of the consequence and not get too deterministic about a single metric or a single variable.”

“I’ve always thought of Wall Street as the buyer of the product that venture capitalists create because the eventual liquidity is either an M&A (merger and acquisition) or an IPO (initial public offering).”

One question to ask before hiring or investing in someone: Is this person going to do this no matter what?

The anticuchos at Cholapink. | Cholapink

items.text:
The anticuchos at Cholapink. | Cholapink

We’ve been covering various NYC restaurants, food, drinks, bars, etc. news intel over on our daily newsletter (please sign up if you haven’t already!), but we’re also making it easier for everyone to catch up by rounding ‘em up here every week (check out August, July, and June’s).

September 11

A new Peruvian spot from a chef and a rapper

Peruvian chef Jaime Pesaque (of notable Lima restaurant Mayta) and Puerto Rican rapper Daddy Yankee (yes) are teaming up to open a new fast-casual Peruvian restaurant in New York City this fall. Cholapink is opening at 32 Spring Street, near Mott Street, in Nolita in October. The menu highlights grilled street food, also known as anticuchos, with ajis (marinades and sauces) like miso-glazed chicken thighs, pineapple gochujang pork belly, yuzu-amarillo fish, and spicy peanut mushrooms.

An NYC taco fave gets private equity funding

NYC’s favorite taqueria chain Los Tacos No. 1 is getting investment money from private equity firm TSG Consumer Partners, as reported by QSR. After the news was announced, people took to commenting on Los Tacos’ Instagram page, worrying about potential quality issues and increased prices (see: the discourse about Salt Hank’s acquisition by food hall behemoth Wonder). The team responded, assuring that they’re “definitely not messing with the tacos,” and that the reason they took the investment is so that they can “keep getting better at it” and expand. The restaurant recently partnered with Gap on an apparel collaboration.

An NYC artist and restaurant owner has died

Lucien Smith, the NYC artist who had revived iconic Chinatown restaurant Food, has died at the age of 37, as reported by Cultured. The restaurant had posted last week that it was temporarily closing.

Fall restaurant season is HERE

Bad news: Summer is unofficially over. Good news: it’s fall preview season! Part one of Eater NY’s most anticipated restaurant openings of the fall is on the website; part two is over on Substack.

An anticipated Hong Kong-style diner finds its address

Turns out chef Lucas Sin is indeed opening his dream cha chaan teng Lok Kee at M Star Cafe in Chinatown, where he’d been popping up this late summer.

Mrs. and Mr. Swift’s NYC night out

Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce dined at Ambassadors Clubhouse on Saturday, September 6, per a rep for the fancy Indian restaurant in Nomad. They dined in one of the private dining rooms, enjoying drinks and food. I’d bet they ordered the tableside whiskey cocktail, the Patiala Peg.

Top Chef winner pops up with bodega preview

Chef Danny Garcia continues previewing his forthcoming Latin halal restaurant, Only Goods, with a pop-up bodega this weekend. It’s taking place at 307 Bedford Avenue, near South Second Street in Williamsburg on Saturday, September 12, from 1 to 5 p.m.

A kaiseki anniversary party

Tribeca kaiseki Muku is celebrating its first anniversary with a special tasting menu this fall, featuring dishes like a rare Japanese sweetfish and harako meshi, a dish of white rice, salmon, and roe. The $375 menu is available through Saturday, October 3.

A 10-year-restaurant collab celebration

To celebrate Fish Cheek’s 10th birthday, the restaurant is teaming up with other NYC restaurants and bars for special collaboration dishes. Starting on Saturday, September 12, find the choo chee michelada and zapp popcorn chicken at Lower East Side cocktail bar Double Chicken Please; the razor clams with nam jim seafood at American Asian Hudson Square restaurant Kiko; the clam pie at both the East Village and Bushwick locations of Ops Pizza; and sliced flaky Thai coconut cake at sibling gluten-free Nolita bakery Bub’s. And then, starting on Monday, September 14, there’s a special burger at Prospect Heights Jewish bistro Gertrude’s.

September 4

A Vietnamese American bakery returns to Brooklyn

Some good news: After baker Doris Hồ-Kane shuttered her Vietnamese American bakery in February, she’s working on bringing back Bạn Bè to its original Carroll Gardens neighborhood.

Hồ-Kane launched a Kickstarter campaign to help fund the opening. She’s aiming to open in November at 115 Columbia Street, at Kane Street, in the Columbia Street Waterfront District.

The resurrected space will have a takeout window and a first-time indoor dine-in space. On deck are pastries and sweets like the beautiful bright-green pandan honeycomb cake and new stuff like pandan lime madeleines and pandan chocolate tiramisu. For savory vegeterian items, look for banh mi, Vietnamese crepes, and summer rolls, along with coffee and tea drinks.

The McNally son ventures into the restaurant world

Keith McNally’s son, George, opens his Tribeca restaurant, Faux, on Thursday, September 3, at 277 Church Street, between White and Franklin streets. McNally (the son) knows the restaurant life well, having worked at his father’s spots like Balthazar and the D.C. location of Minetta Tavern. Faux’s chef Kristina Ramos (who worked at Minetta in D.C.) is cooking up a coastal French menu, with highlights including broiled oysters and steak frites. The ground-floor restaurant includes a downstairs bar, Prevz, with late-night food and a bouncer. Book restaurant reservations on OpenTable.

Buy stellar baked goods for a good cause

Expert baker Natasha Pickowicz is hosting a community bake sale this weekend to raise money for Queens nonprofit Make the Road New York. Our Little Bake Sale features chefs like Pickowicz herself, Zoë Kanan of Elbow Bread, Morgan Knight of Saint Street Cakes, Flynn McCarry of Cove, Ali Domrongchai, and many others. It’s free to attend; each pastry is worth one ticket, which is $10. The event, which is a partnership with indie food publication Cake Zine, takes place on Sunday, September 6, from 3 to 5 p.m. at Little Island, the park on Pier 55 along Hudson River Park at West 13th Street.

Two NYC restaurants take over Times Square Red Lobster

A restaurant group behind NYC restaurants, including American brasserie the Smith and pizzeria Parla, is taking over the recently shuttered Red Lobster in Times Square, as reported by the New York Post. The business plans to open a fifth location of the Smith and a pizza-slice spinoff of Parla at a two-floor address at 582 Seventh Avenue, between West 41st and 42nd streets, set to debut in 2028.

A bread bakery grows in Crown Heights

In more bakery news, Apt. 2 Bread, a micro-bakery best known for its focaccia, is working on opening a bread-focused bakery named Boots Bread in Crown Heights. Carla Finley is teaming up with Megan Wang for the new venture. When the bakery opens, expect all sorts of breads made with regional grains.

What’s happening with Food?

Looks like Chinatown restaurant Food, the revitalized Chinatown restaurant now run by artist Lucien Smith, seems to have “closed until further notice,” per its Instagram.

A Radio Bakery branch is temporarily closed

The Greenpoint location of Radio Bakery is temporarily closing for renovations, from Tuesday, September 1, through Monday, September 21. To help ease the demand, the Prospect Heights location is staying open later (until 6 p.m.) through Sunday, September 13.

An Austin bar pop-up worth going to

One of my personal favorite bars ever, Austin’s Nickel City, is coming to New York City for a pop-up this month. Owner Travis Tober is taking over the bar of Romeo’s in the East Village, on Wednesday, September 9, from 8 to 11 p.m., with Dr Pepper Old Fashioneds, Mexican martinis, and more.

If you’re going to Harry Styles…

If your Labor Day weekend plans include seeing Harry Styles at Madison Square Garden this Friday, September 4, and/or Saturday, September 5, we’ve got a handy guide for you, at least when it comes to drinking and eating. Pro tip: Make sure you’re seated/standing by the time opener Jamie XX plays his final song, because Harry and company take the stage at the same time to kick off the show.

items.text:
When it comes to finding gifts for people who love to cook, I stand by a simple gift shopping mantra: Know what your giftee likes, and then expand upon (or improve) their area of interest. Meaning, if they’re always tracking down rare spices, gift them a pirate’s hoard of blends from one of our favorite places to buy spices online; if they love to bake, equip them with a charming set of nontoxic, miniature muffin baking pans. And so on and so forth; basically, pay attention to what needs an upgrade in their life (there’s a good chance it’s cooking utensils) and which knives aren’t cutting it in their rotation.

items.title: The Best New Restaurants in Queens
items.summary: Astoria now has a spot to satisfy soulful cravings for long-simmered Korean seolleongtang (ox bone soup). Jin Broth is a takeout counter inside the Marquee
items.text:
Astoria now has a spot to satisfy soulful cravings for long-simmered Korean seolleongtang (ox bone soup). Jin Broth is a takeout counter inside the Marquee Astoria banquet hall, which opened in May. Amid business conventions, there’s marvelous seolleongtang: thick, white, and almost creamy from all the collagen that’s seeped out from hours of simmering beef bones. It comes with the customary fixings of scallions, sea salt, and pepper so everyone can season it to their liking. Tender beef also appears in the suyuk (boiled beef slices with dips) and what the restaurant calls lasagna dumplings: squares of dumpling stuffing with the wrapper on the top and bottom.

After a decades-long hustle, Burmese Bites chef and owner Myo Lin Thway has finally opened the full-service restaurant of his dreams. The former buffet-style Point Brazil in Astoria has transformed into a cool, bustling space with quick, kind service. All the bestsellers from Thway’s days at street festivals, Queens Night Market, and Queens Center Mall now rest in beautiful, colorful ceramics and thatched wood plateware. The must-orders: the assorted palatas like the chicken curry that kickstarted the business; tea leaf salad; ohno kauswe (coconut chicken noodle soup); mohinga (ground fish noodle soup); and crispy eel chile fries.

Xiaozhan is a fantastic rice noodle soup spot with a sauce bar in Flushing, which opened in May. All ten noodle soups are served in mini clay pots with bundles of slippery, slurpy, bouncy rice noodles; vegetables; and protein options such as fish, beef, shrimp, and chicken. The soup bases vary from mushrooms to assorted chile preparations (charred, pickled, oil), but the passionfruit stands out. It has a lovely balance of robust flavors — sour, spicy, savory — brightened up with passion fruit and lemon. And if you want more spiciness or umami, head to the sauce bar. The space is tiny, and wait times can exceed an hour, so go during off-peak hours.

Northwestern Queens can now grab some good Nigerian jollof and suya with the opening of the D.C.-based takeout chain Disbe Good, which opened inside the Sunnyside Eats ghost kitchen in May. The jollof is fluffy, tomato-based, and subtly spicy. But the charcoal-grilled smokiness of the suya is loud and proud — whether you opt for the beef, chicken, or lamb. And all the meats are halal. Every order comes with an extra helping of yaji, their quality suya spice blend of peanut, smoked paprika, and chile pepper, so you can use any leftovers for your own home cooking.

Woodside has gained a thoughtful restaurant that pushes the boundaries of typical Japanese American restaurants in New York with Tomoni, which opened in April. Lunch sets include common premium offerings like wagyu or eel donburi, but the perfectly cooked protein portions are generous. But Tomoni also offers misozuke cream cheese, which has been marinated in miso for two days and served with nori and wasabi; it’s delightful: nutty and slightly sweet. There’s also the raw octopus (a small bowl of shredded octopus in a slightly vinegary seasoning) and natto (the sticky, stringy fermented soybeans usually eaten at home). It’s served with rice, sauce, a raw pasteurized egg, a couple of slices of grilled eel, tamagoyaki, and miso soup.

What looks small and divey from the front opens up into a large Chinese banquet hall-type space. Peruse a massive menu of Cantonese classics that had been sorely missing in NYC’s newest Chinatown. Fresh lobster is coated in a garlicky brown sauce. Fried whole anchovies are tossed in salt and pepper. Stellar snow pea sprouts get braised in a light savory broth, topped with fried shrimp, and served in a cast iron pot. Head over for weekday lunch specials ($14-17) on entrees like beef stew with radish and chicken with cashews — all served with soup and rice.

A new Uzbek restaurant has been doling out traditional dishes in Rego Park since April. Registan Plov Center lives up to its name with a plov that’s freshly made daily in the mornings. It’s a dome of rice, chickpeas, lamb, and cubed carrots with pops of sweetness from raisins — all tantalizingly slicked with lamb fat. Get the grilled lamb ribs, too. It’s served on a mountain of sliced lemon and tomato, topped with potato chips and a flourish of sliced onions. Wash it all down with kompot, a light seasonal fruit juice; it’s mixed berries for summer.

On the weekends, all the Forest Hills families are at the massive new location of Turkish American chain Zara, which opened in May. Of the many highlights, the huge complimentary balloon bread — that’s the length of an arm and puffed up straight out of the open-flame oven — might be the greatest. Rip into it and dip into spreads like labneh, hummus, and babaganoush. Or wrap it around grilled kababs, short ribs, and steaks. Leave room for desserts. The tas kadayif is made fresh to order: pan-fried pastry stuffed with walnuts and honey, which is served with vanilla ice cream.

blocks.x: Astoria now has a spot to satisfy soulful cravings for long-simmered Korean seolleongtang (ox bone soup). Jin Broth is a takeout counter inside the Marquee Astoria banquet hall, which opened in May. Amid business conventions, there’s marvelous seolleongtang: thick, white, and almost creamy from all the collagen that’s seeped out from hours of simmering beef bones. It comes with the customary fixings of scallions, sea salt, and pepper so everyone can season it to their liking. Tender beef also appears in the suyuk (boiled beef slices with dips) and what the restaurant calls lasagna dumplings: squares of dumpling stuffing with the wrapper on the top and bottom.

items.title: Are AI-Made Reservations Fair?
items.author: Sam Stone
items.summary: Welcome to Open Tab, a weekly roundup of the news, gossip, and stories that have stayed open in my tabs all week. Last time we covered the end of ‘Chicken Shop
items.text:
Welcome to Open Tab, a weekly roundup of the news, gossip, and stories that have stayed open in my tabs all week. Last time we covered the end of ‘Chicken Shop Date.’

Welcome back to Open Tab. Labor Day weekend was excuse enough for me to make salmon tacos with pineapple-chile salsa—always a hit—followed by a fluffy, aromatic olive oil cake. I’ve found myself cooking at home almost exclusively in recent weeks, but, in no particular order, here are the New York Restaurants I’ve been meaning to hit: Dean’s, Hommali, Kirbee’s, Graciela, and El Califa de Leon. Make of that list what you will.

This week marks 25 years since the attacks on 9/11—many in the food world are remembering Windows on the World, the restaurant opened on the top floors of the North Tower. CNN also released a documentary on the restaurant, which was at one time the highest-grossing standalone restaurant in the country.

Another fascinating read: Ruby Tandoh in the New Yorker on Saudi Arabia’s quest to rebrand as a culinary capital which includes, among other things, the introduction of Michelin stars last year. Michelin has been evaluating more and more cities, often partnering with (read: getting paid by) local tourism boards who recognize that the distinction can attract a real wave of tourists to the area. But when I interviewed him a couple years ago, Gwendal Poullennec, international director of the Michelin Guide, insisted that the guide’s expansion wasn’t about the money—it was about finding more cities with “culinary potential” than ever before.

Oh, also they’re doing $60 loaves of rye bread now. Oy.

Also in this week’s Open Tab: the people using AI agents to score reservations, what exactly are ultraprocessed foods?, and the eternal question: Is it ever ok to bring your own seasonings to restaurants?

AI agents? I have reservations

This week’s addition to the AI hellscape? Personal AI agents. Meta released Muse, and Instinct continues to gain traction. These are agents that can respond to emails, book plane tickets, secure you a spot in a workout class, arrange and rearrange your calendar, and, yes, make grab that impossible-to-get dinner reservation. Hypothetically.

Using AI agents to nab tough reservations may also get you banned from reservation platforms, as one user found out this week. The way these agents work is by spamming the reservation platform hundreds of times per hour for hours on end. The reservation platforms flag that as suspicious activity, and may ban your account.

When I reached out to Resy for comment, a spokesperson clarified that the company doesn’t permit “unapproved third-party bots or AI agents to independently access or interact with the Resy platform.” That’s not to say the company is anti-AI—it’s recently announced integrations with ChatGPT and Claude. But rather, it says, Resy wants to maintain a “fair reservation experience for diners.”

And that’s really the crux of the issue; it’s not hard to imagine a day in the not-too-distant future when AI agents can work within a platform's terms of service (in fact, that day may have actually been earlier this week) grabbing the toughest tables the second they become available. It’s an undeniable upping of the ante in the already impossible reservations war. What are non-agent-assisted restaurant lovers to do? How can restaurants, many dependent on these platforms to stay booked, respond? Is this the beginning of a golden age for walk-in only spots?

What exactly makes a food ultraprocessed?

This week, California approved a landmark bill that establishes a process for which foods may label themselves as non-ultraprocessed. This comes after the state was the first in the nation to put forth a solid definition of what exactly an ultraprocessed food is. Although there’s been a lot of talk about ultraprocessed foods (or UPFs)—mostly stemming from the MAHA movement—there’s not a true consensus on how to delineate which foods are ultraprocessed and which aren’t.

I mean, sure, maybe you simply know it when you see it: an apple is not ultraprocessed. Gently glowing, fire-engine red flamin’ hot cheetos boxed mac and cheese is ultraprocessed.

At the federal level, the US is still in the process of drawing up an official definition, but around the world, several definitions are held as true. Brazilian researchers define UPFs as all foods with industrial ingredients like sweeteners or emulsifiers. Research group Healthy Eating Research says they’re foods “processed to the extent that they are no longer recognizable as their original plant/animal source.”

Though there isn’t a firm categorization (yet), we’re already beginning to see colossal food companies respond to the discourse. PepsiCo is reportedly shifting focus to fresh foods instead of processed ones, and some cereal companies have stopped using artificial dyes. All good stuff, but I will say this: You can pry my flamin’ hot cheetos mac and cheese out of my cold, dead, cholesterol-clogged hands.

Some people bring their own birthday cakes to restaurants. Others bring their own bottle of wine to enjoy with dinner. And then there are the people who bring their own seasonings to restaurants. It’s a controversial topic, but for those who don’t leave the house without their pocket Maldon, their Calabrian chili oil, their fancy olive oil it’s really no question at all. Read Maggie Hennessy’s intriguing piece on Bon Appétit for more.

items.title: Fukushima’s Old Farming Rituals Come to Life in Haga Hideo’s Photography
items.summary: During the 1950s the photographer Haga Hideo captured traditional folk festivals in Fukushima Prefecture. Now the memories in his work have come back home,
items.text:
During the 1950s the photographer Haga Hideo captured traditional folk festivals in Fukushima Prefecture. Now the memories in his work have come back home, with the presentation of his photographic data to locals who are already putting it to work to bring these traditions back to life.

Worshipping Tanokami: The Deity of Abundant Harvests

Before becoming a professional photographer, the pioneering folklore photographer Haga Hideo (1921–2022) worked as a translator at a news agency. That career came to an end in 1952 when the agency disbanded. For a change of scene, he headed to Fukushima Prefecture, where his father was from. While staying with relatives in what is now the city of Iwaki, he encountered a New Year ritual performed among farming families.

Prior to Japan’s rapid economic development in the years after World War II, folk beliefs in the tanokami rice deity were alive and well in many parts of the country. In Fukushima, the family patriarch and his eldest son would gather the straw from the rice harvested the previous fall to create a yorishiro, an object to beckon a deity, to welcome Shōgatsu-sama, the spirit thought to bring bountiful crops. In spring, this spirit would reappear in the rice paddies to make the rice ripen; it would then leave after the fall harvest, returning to the mountains where it dwelled.

The idea of an invisible deity responsible for the bounty of nature inspired Haga, who turned his camera lens to deity-welcoming ceremonies and their carefully crafted ritual implements and offerings. Casting a closer eye on this unadorned spiritual culture, he was reminded of marebito, the concept of a divine spirit visiting from the “other world” that he had learned about from the folklorist and ethnologist Orikuchi Shinobu (1887–1953) during his university studies.

The altar for worshipping Shōgatsu-sama on the first day of the new year. (© Haga Hideo)

A ceremony to pray for a good harvest, performed after a paddy dried out during winter has been worked with a hoe in preparation for planting. (© Haga Hideo)

Preparing mochibana, bits of mochi pounded rice threaded onto branches, as a stand-in for Shōgatsu-sama, on January 13. (© Haga Hideo)

A divination ritual conducted on the evening of January 14. Twelve soybeans are roasted in the irori sunken hearth and used to predict the weather for the coming year according to the degree of charring. (© Haga Hideo)

Torigoya is conducted even today on koshōgatsu, January 15. Bamboo, straw, and New Year decorations are burned to return Shōgatsu-sama to the heavens. (© Haga Hideo)

Warmed by hearty oden stew, children gather in a hut to sing a song to drive away birds, which eat the grain the fields, in the hope of an abundant harvest. (© Haga Hideo)

Passing On the Traditions of Iwaki

In the foreword to Tanokami: Nihon no inasaku girei (Deity of the Rice Paddies: The Rice Cultivation Rituals of Japan), Haga’s first collection of photos taken in Iwaki, he explained why he had chosen to pursue this work there.

For 2,000 years, the Japanese people have grown rice, around which the belief in tanokami and associated rituals has developed. Many Japanese customs and myths have been influenced by tanokami, providing insight into how rice cultivation rituals are reflected in daily life and social structures . . . Today, modern science has made good harvests possible without the intervention of tanokami. Progress in agricultural technology and the modernization of farm life are rapidly eroding traditional village society, in which religious beliefs, crop production, and entertainment were intertwined. This is a last opportunity to record the rituals associated with rice production for posterity.

As Haga had foreseen, the rituals around rice growing were rapidly becoming simplified or had disappeared altogether. Meanwhile, the significance of rites centering around tanokami, such as Hiroshima Prefecture’s Mibu no Hana Taue and Ishikawa Prefecture’s Oku-Noto Aenokoto, has been recognized with their collective inscription by UNESCO as Intangible Cultural Heritage. Haga, who made recording folklore for posterity his lifework, passed away in 2022 at the age of 101.

Iwaki, where Haga got his start as a folklore photographer, is today on the verge of losing its traditional farming culture. The Iwaki City Museum of Folklore and Traditional Housing, which opened in 1999, is leading efforts to preserve what is left of those traditions. The museum collects and displays all manner of artifacts related to local life.

Five traditional thatched-roof houses, dismantled and transported from various parts of Iwaki, have been re-erected in the museum’s vast grounds. Meticulously preserved, they reproduce a premodern farm village. On display inside the houses are farming tools of the era; visitors can also try their hand at working in the fields and paddies outside. Iwaki schoolchildren visit here as part of their social studies lessons, and on weekends, adults can participate in workshops to learn about the local culture.

The permanent exhibit showcases farm life from the Edo period (1603–1868) to the present. (© Uzawa Akihiko)

Farm tools and artifacts, including a life-sized figure (at left) created to protect the village from evil, have been collected from various parts of Iwaki. (© Uzawa Akihiko)

A traditional home from the latter half of the nineteenth century stands in the park. (© Uzawa Akihiko)

The interior is mostly untouched. (© Uzawa Akihiko)

Mochibana prepared by children are displayed. (© Uzawa Akihiko)

Top: The Jangara Nenbutsu Odori folk entertainment performed during the midsummer bon period. Bottom: A child is taught how to make a New Year decoration. (Courtesy Iwaki City Museum of Folklore and Traditional Housing)

In the summer of 2026, Haga’s son Haga Hinata visited the folklore museum to donate 46 film rolls’ worth of digitalized photo data, to help teach local history. Worshipping Tanokami: The Deity of Abundant Harvests

Before becoming a professional photographer, the pioneering folklore photographer Haga Hideo (1921–2022) worked as a translator at a news agency. That career came to an end in 1952 when the agency disbanded. For a change of scene, he headed to Fukushima Prefecture, where his father was from. While staying with relatives in what is now the city of Iwaki, he encountered a New Year ritual performed among farming families.

Prior to Japan’s rapid economic development in the years after World War II, folk beliefs in the tanokami rice deity were alive and well in many parts of the country. In Fukushima, the family patriarch and his eldest son would gather the straw from the rice harvested the previous fall to create a yorishiro, an object to beckon a deity, to welcome Shōgatsu-sama, the spirit thought to bring bountiful crops. In spring, this spirit would reappear in the rice paddies to make the rice ripen; it would then leave after the fall harvest, returning to the mountains where it dwelled.

The idea of an invisible deity responsible for the bounty of nature inspired Haga, who turned his camera lens to deity-welcoming ceremonies and their carefully crafted ritual implements and offerings. Casting a closer eye on this unadorned spiritual culture, he was reminded of marebito, the concept of a divine spirit visiting from the “other world” that he had learned about from the folklorist and ethnologist Orikuchi Shinobu (1887–1953) during his university studies.

Passing On the Traditions of Iwaki

In the foreword to Tanokami: Nihon no inasaku girei (Deity of the Rice Paddies: The Rice Cultivation Rituals of Japan), Haga’s first collection of photos taken in Iwaki, he explained why he had chosen to pursue this work there.

For 2,000 years, the Japanese people have grown rice, around which the belief in tanokami and associated rituals has developed. Many Japanese customs and myths have been influenced by tanokami, providing insight into how rice cultivation rituals are reflected in daily life and social structures . . . Today, modern science has made good harvests possible without the intervention of tanokami. Progress in agricultural technology and the modernization of farm life are rapidly eroding traditional village society, in which religious beliefs, crop production, and entertainment were intertwined. This is a last opportunity to record the rituals associated with rice production for posterity.

As Haga had foreseen, the rituals around rice growing were rapidly becoming simplified or had disappeared altogether. Meanwhile, the significance of rites centering around tanokami, such as Hiroshima Prefecture’s Mibu no Hana Taue and Ishikawa Prefecture’s Oku-Noto Aenokoto, has been recognized with their collective inscription by UNESCO as Intangible Cultural Heritage. Haga, who made recording folklore for posterity his lifework, passed away in 2022 at the age of 101.

The Iwaki City Museum of Folklore and Traditional Housing, which opened in 1999, is leading efforts to preserve what is left of those traditions. The museum collects and displays all manner of artifacts related to local life.

Five traditional thatched-roof houses, dismantled and transported from various parts of Iwaki, have been re-erected in the museum’s vast grounds. Meticulously preserved, they reproduce a premodern farm village. On display inside the houses are farming tools of the era; visitors can also try their hand at working in the fields and paddies outside. Iwaki schoolchildren visit here as part of their social studies lessons, and on weekends, adults can participate in workshops to learn about the local culture.

items.title: Must-Try Spots For Noodle Lovers
items.author: Holyn Thigpen
items.summary: Humans have been slurping and savoring noodles for centuries, with the first recorded noodle dish recorded during China’s Eastern Han period (25–220 CE). In
items.text:
Humans have been slurping and savoring noodles for centuries, with the first recorded noodle dish recorded during China’s Eastern Han period (25–220 CE). In fact, noodles would go on to become inextricable from ancient Chinese culture, with a wheat-based version emerging as a staple of the Han dynasty. Centuries later, noodle-making would hit Europe, transforming the cuisines of Italy during the Middle Ages and Germany in the early 18th century. The English word “noodle” itself goes back to the 18th century, borrowed by the English from the German “nudel.”


Whatever you call them, one thing remains certain: Love of noodles transcends culture and country. Jacques Cousteau once said that the sea was “the great unifier ... man’s only hope,” but did he ever consider the power of a steaming bowl of ramen? For this delicious guide, we’ve noodled on the best of the best around the world—places where mind-bending broths and eccentric histories collide to create unforgettable dining experiences.

1. Hrimnir Ramen 📍 Oslo, Norway


This Oslo eatery puts a uniquely Norwegian spin on traditional Japanese ramen, using seasonal local ingredients found from the fjords to the mountains. Opened by Norwegian-American microbiologist David Quist in 2019, Hrimnir places a special focus on fermented ingredients, with jars of preserved lemons, pickled plums, and pear vinegar lining the walls. The noodles are handmade in house with emmer wheat or tokornkveite, a heritage grain that gives them a uniquely nutty flavor.

2. Phở Hàng Trống 📍 Hanoi, Vietnam


Hanoi is considered the birthplace of Vietnam’s staple noodle soup, phở, and in the living room of home chef Ms. Minh, you’ll find some of the very best in the country. She’s been selling phở in Hanoi for decades but was forced to take her business inside in 2017, when the city started cracking down on street vendors.


At plastic tables, visitors to Ms. Minh’s home can enjoy traditional, northern-style phở (which has lighter, clearer broth than that in the south). She serves her noodles with jars of homemade chili sauce and pickled garlic, plus the option of dipping Chinese youtiao doughnuts in the hot broth.


3. Inari Soba Mansei 📍 Tokyo, Japan


This small soba shop dates back to the early 1600s, where it appears in the legend of Takuzousu, a Buddhist monk and kitsune, or shapeshifting fox-spirit. It’s said that Takuzousu frequented this very shop, where the coins he paid with supposedly turned into leaves once their magic had worn off.


You’d never know the restaurant’s legendary history from the outside, but inside, you’ll find a bronze bell from the original Takuzousu shrine displayed in glass. The menu, too, pays tribute to the kitsune by serving aburaage, a fried tofu believed to be foxes’ favorite food.

4. Pekin Noodle Parlor 📍 Butte, Montana


Pekin Noodle Parlor is the oldest continuously-operating Chinese restaurant in the U.S., opened in 1911 in what was once a thriving Chinatown. Passed down through the same family for generations, Pekin radiates old-school charm: A flickering, neon sign welcomes visitors into a dimly-lit space with orange booths and individual eating cubicles, where food arrives by trolley. The parlor’s main draw is the Chinese-American classic, chop suey, but it also serves up a mean chow mein and chicken noodle soup.


5. Mie Lethek Garuda 📍 Srandakan, Indonesia


In this traditional factory, cows turn a huge mortar that grinds dried cassava and sweet potatoes into flour for mie lethek, the region’s signature noodle variety. Mie lethek translates to “ugly noodles,” an apt name for these squiggly gray creations. But what they lack in beauty, they make up for in flavor: sweeter than your average noodle, with a pleasant, chewy texture.


Yasir Feri, Mie Lethek Garuda’s owner, is the grandson of the noodle’s creators, a Yemeni/Chinese couple who first opened up shop in the 1940s. After the cows have created the flour, Feri and his factory workers mix and press the dough by hand, then leave the finished noodles to dry in the sun before bringing them to the market. (The cows are also given sweet grass in return for their hard work.)

6. Pure Love Diner Bar 📍 Taipei, Taiwan


Colorful neon signs welcome you into this ’80s-themed den of vice (and noodles), complete with red lighting, disco balls, and antique furniture. The diner is an homage to Taipei’s old-school karaoke bars, known as “grandpa shops” for their older—and often flirtatious—patrons, though without any of the original bars’ suspicious activity.


Here, it’s all about enjoying the kitschy ambiance and chowing down on Taiwanese classics like braised pork over rice, oyster soup, fried chicken, and deep-fried noodles in satay sauce. Plus, there’s still a karaoke machine in the corner!

7. Fideus de Vermar 📍 Binissalem, Spain


This small town of Binissalem celebrates its rich wine heritage with the annual Festa des Vermar, which includes (among plenty of wine-based activities) huge cauldrons of short noodles, slow-cooked meats, red wine, and aromatic spices. This traditional local paella, called fideus de vermar, serves all 1,400 of the town’s residents during the festival, turning the main square into a lively picnic spot.

8. Bamonte’s 📍 Brooklyn, New York


Founded by immigrants in 1900, this family institution holds the distinction of being Brooklyn’s oldest Italian restaurant. It was once a favorite meeting spot of the New York mafia, as well as a setting for the fictional New Jersey mob in “The Sopranos.” Other (more law-abiding) Italian-Americans of note, such as Robert De Niro and Frank Sinatra, have dined here, and the restaurant honors its many famous guests with framed photos on the walls.


While New York City has grown exceedingly expensive, Bamonte’s has kept its Italian classics surprisingly affordable, and crowd-pleasers like the rigatoni alla vodka and linguine with red clam sauce keep people coming back year after year.

9. Khanom Jeen Pa Mai 📍 Phuket Town, Thailand


Thin white rice noodles called khanom jeen are a staple throughout Thailand, where they’re served with various spicy curries, meats, and vegetables. At this unassuming eatery in Phuket Town, customization reaches new heights with a lineup of everything from crispy dried fish to pickled mustard greens to pineapple slices.

10. Hawker Chan Soya Sauce Chicken Rice & Noodle 📍 Singapore


For about $3, you can enjoy a Michelin-star meal at this Singapore noodle shop. Owner and chef Chan Hon Meng first opened Hawker Chan as a food-court stall, where it became famous with his “secret,” Cantonese-style chicken marinade. The flavorful braised meat is served over char siew noodles, rice, or hor fun noodles with stir-fried veggies and braised eggs.


After Meng took home a Michelin star in 2016 (which he at first assumed was a practical joke), he turned Hawker Chan into a full-scale restaurant right next to where his humble stall once stood. Since then, other locations have opened in Thailand, Kazakhstan, Laos, and Malaysia, with more still on the way.

11. Lin Heung Tea House 📍 Hong Kong


Founded in the late 19th century, Lin Heung may just be Hong Kong’s oldest dim sum spot. It still does things the old-school way, too, with servers wheeling trolleys stacked high with bamboo steamers and calling out what dishes are up. Simply head over to the trolley and load up on what looks good to you, whether it’s rice noodle rolls, shrimp dumplings, pork ribs, or congee. The tea house can get quite crowded, so sharing a table with (or even befriending) fellow customers is simply a part of the experience.

12. Matsuka Seimen Noodle Factory 📍 Kurashiki, Japan


This gray shed functions mainly as a noodle factory, but during certain times of day, it changes gears to serve up freshly-cooked udon topped with eggs, scallions, and chili oil. Regulars swear by the kamatama: piping hot udon paired with nothing but a raw egg (cooked by the noodles) and a drizzle of soy sauce. Matsuka Seimen’s tiny kitchen also churns out a rich curry ramen made with fatty slivers of pork and soba noodles in a delicate green tea broth.


If you’re lucky, while you wait for your meal, you’ll witness the Matsuka family’s rather unusual noodle-kneading technique: A large tray of dough is covered in cloth and placed on the floor, where a family member walks all over it in special socks.

13. Bún Riêu Gánh 📍 Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam


On the busy streets of Ho Chi Minh City, Mrs. Mai Thi Lien serves up hefty ladles of simmering red broth from a massive pot on the sidewalk. Bún riêu, the noodle soup for which her restaurant is named, is made with rice vermicelli noodles and shrimp or pork mixed with crab paste, plus crispy tofu, huyet (coagulated pork blood), and herbs for garnishing. Mrs. Lien puts her own spin on the classic dish by pairing it with a tamarind fish sauce with sliced chili, giving it a distinctly southern Vietnamese flavor.

blocks.x: Humans have been slurping and savoring noodles for centuries, with the first recorded noodle dish recorded during China’s Eastern Han period (25–220 CE). In fact, noodles would go on to become inextricable from ancient Chinese culture, with a wheat-based version emerging as a staple of the Han dynasty. Centuries later, noodle-making would hit Europe, transforming the cuisines of Italy during the Middle Ages and Germany in the early 18th century. The English word “noodle” itself goes back to the 18th century, borrowed by the English from the German “nudel.”

Whatever you call them, one thing remains certain: Love of noodles transcends culture and country. Jacques Cousteau once said that the sea was “the great unifier ... man’s only hope,” but did he ever consider the power of a steaming bowl of ramen? For this delicious guide, we’ve noodled on the best of the best around the world—places where mind-bending broths and eccentric histories collide to create unforgettable dining experiences.
1. Hrimnir Ramen 📍 Oslo, Norway

This Oslo eatery puts a uniquely Norwegian spin on traditional Japanese ramen, using seasonal local ingredients found from the fjords to the mountains. Opened by Norwegian-American microbiologist David Quist in 2019, Hrimnir places a special focus on fermented ingredients, with jars of preserved lemons, pickled plums, and pear vinegar lining the walls. The noodles are handmade in house with emmer wheat or tokornkveite, a heritage grain that gives them a uniquely nutty flavor.
2. Phở Hàng Trống 📍 Hanoi, Vietnam

Hanoi is considered the birthplace of Vietnam’s staple noodle soup, phở, and in the living room of home chef Ms. Minh, you’ll find some of the very best in the country. She’s been selling phở in Hanoi for decades but was forced to take her business inside in 2017, when the city started cracking down on street vendors.

At plastic tables, visitors to Ms. Minh’s home can enjoy traditional, northern-style phở (which has lighter, clearer broth than that in the south). She serves her noodles with jars of homemade chili sauce and pickled garlic, plus the option of dipping Chinese youtiao doughnuts in the hot broth.
3. Inari Soba Mansei 📍 Tokyo, Japan

This small soba shop dates back to the early 1600s, where it appears in the legend of Takuzousu, a Buddhist monk and kitsune, or shapeshifting fox-spirit. It’s said that Takuzousu frequented this very shop, where the coins he paid with supposedly turned into leaves once their magic had worn off.

You’d never know the restaurant’s legendary history from the outside, but inside, you’ll find a bronze bell from the original Takuzousu shrine displayed in glass. The menu, too, pays tribute to the kitsune by serving aburaage, a fried tofu believed to be foxes’ favorite food.
4. Pekin Noodle Parlor 📍 Butte, Montana

Pekin Noodle Parlor is the oldest continuously-operating Chinese restaurant in the U.S., opened in 1911 in what was once a thriving Chinatown. Passed down through the same family for generations, Pekin radiates old-school charm: A flickering, neon sign welcomes visitors into a dimly-lit space with orange booths and individual eating cubicles, where food arrives by trolley. The parlor’s main draw is the Chinese-American classic, chop suey, but it also serves up a mean chow mein and chicken noodle soup.
5. Mie Lethek Garuda 📍 Srandakan, Indonesia

In this traditional factory, cows turn a huge mortar that grinds dried cassava and sweet potatoes into flour for mie lethek, the region’s signature noodle variety. Mie lethek translates to “ugly noodles,” an apt name for these squiggly gray creations. But what they lack in beauty, they make up for in flavor: sweeter than your average noodle, with a pleasant, chewy texture.

Yasir Feri, Mie Lethek Garuda’s owner, is the grandson of the noodle’s creators, a Yemeni/Chinese couple who first opened up shop in the 1940s. After the cows have created the flour, Feri and his factory workers mix and press the dough by hand, then leave the finished noodles to dry in the sun before bringing them to the market. (The cows are also given sweet grass in return for their hard work.)
6. Pure Love Diner Bar 📍 Taipei, Taiwan

Colorful neon signs welcome you into this ’80s-themed den of vice (and noodles), complete with red lighting, disco balls, and antique furniture. The diner is an homage to Taipei’s old-school karaoke bars, known as “grandpa shops” for their older—and often flirtatious—patrons, though without any of the original bars’ suspicious activity.

Here, it’s all about enjoying the kitschy ambiance and chowing down on Taiwanese classics like braised pork over rice, oyster soup, fried chicken, and deep-fried noodles in satay sauce. Plus, there’s still a karaoke machine in the corner!
7. Fideus de Vermar 📍 Binissalem, Spain

This small town of Binissalem celebrates its rich wine heritage with the annual Festa des Vermar, which includes (among plenty of wine-based activities) huge cauldrons of short noodles, slow-cooked meats, red wine, and aromatic spices. This traditional local paella, called fideus de vermar, serves all 1,400 of the town’s residents during the festival, turning the main square into a lively picnic spot.
8. Bamonte’s 📍 Brooklyn, New York

Founded by immigrants in 1900, this family institution holds the distinction of being Brooklyn’s oldest Italian restaurant. It was once a favorite meeting spot of the New York mafia, as well as a setting for the fictional New Jersey mob in “The Sopranos.” Other (more law-abiding) Italian-Americans of note, such as Robert De Niro and Frank Sinatra, have dined here, and the restaurant honors its many famous guests with framed photos on the walls.

While New York City has grown exceedingly expensive, Bamonte’s has kept its Italian classics surprisingly affordable, and crowd-pleasers like the rigatoni alla vodka and linguine with red clam sauce keep people coming back year after year.
9. Khanom Jeen Pa Mai 📍 Phuket Town, Thailand

Thin white rice noodles called khanom jeen are a staple throughout Thailand, where they’re served with various spicy curries, meats, and vegetables. At this unassuming eatery in Phuket Town, customization reaches new heights with a lineup of everything from crispy dried fish to pickled mustard greens to pineapple slices.
10. Hawker Chan Soya Sauce Chicken Rice & Noodle 📍 Singapore

For about $3, you can enjoy a Michelin-star meal at this Singapore noodle shop. Owner and chef Chan Hon Meng first opened Hawker Chan as a food-court stall, where it became famous with his “secret,” Cantonese-style chicken marinade. The flavorful braised meat is served over char siew noodles, rice, or hor fun noodles with stir-fried veggies and braised eggs.

After Meng took home a Michelin star in 2016 (which he at first assumed was a practical joke), he turned Hawker Chan into a full-scale restaurant right next to where his humble stall once stood. Since then, other locations have opened in Thailand, Kazakhstan, Laos, and Malaysia, with more still on the way.
11. Lin Heung Tea House 📍 Hong Kong

Founded in the late 19th century, Lin Heung may just be Hong Kong’s oldest dim sum spot. It still does things the old-school way, too, with servers wheeling trolleys stacked high with bamboo steamers and calling out what dishes are up. Simply head over to the trolley and load up on what looks good to you, whether it’s rice noodle rolls, shrimp dumplings, pork ribs, or congee. The tea house can get quite crowded, so sharing a table with (or even befriending) fellow customers is simply a part of the experience.
12. Matsuka Seimen Noodle Factory 📍 Kurashiki, Japan

This gray shed functions mainly as a noodle factory, but during certain times of day, it changes gears to serve up freshly-cooked udon topped with eggs, scallions, and chili oil. Regulars swear by the kamatama: piping hot udon paired with nothing but a raw egg (cooked by the noodles) and a drizzle of soy sauce. Matsuka Seimen’s tiny kitchen also churns out a rich curry ramen made with fatty slivers of pork and soba noodles in a delicate green tea broth.

If you’re lucky, while you wait for your meal, you’ll witness the Matsuka family’s rather unusual noodle-kneading technique: A large tray of dough is covered in cloth and placed on the floor, where a family member walks all over it in special socks.
13. Bún Riêu Gánh 📍 Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam

On the busy streets of Ho Chi Minh City, Mrs. Mai Thi Lien serves up hefty ladles of simmering red broth from a massive pot on the sidewalk. Bún riêu, the noodle soup for which her restaurant is named, is made with rice vermicelli noodles and shrimp or pork mixed with crab paste, plus crispy tofu, huyet (coagulated pork blood), and herbs for garnishing. Mrs. Lien puts her own spin on the classic dish by pairing it with a tamarind fish sauce with sliced chili, giving it a distinctly southern Vietnamese flavor.

items.title: Hull stun Chelsea with Mohamed Belloumi double before João Pedro rescues a point
items.author: Jacob Steinberg at Stamford Bridge
items.summary: The chants from the away end about winning the league were sung in jest, but Hull continue to show they are here to stay. Sergej Jakirovic’s dogged,
items.text:
The chants from the away end about winning the league were sung in jest, but Hull continue to show they are here to stay. Sergej Jakirovic’s dogged, intelligent side are third in the Premier League after extending their unbeaten start to four games and can even count themselves unfortunate not to have beaten another of the Big Six after pushing Chelsea to the limit in an absorbing battle at a frustrated Stamford Bridge.

Hull were 2-1 up at half-time and they had the chances to snatch the points during the second half. It took two big saves from Emiliano Martínez to prevent an upset, but this was not a good day for the Chelsea goalkeeper or his new teammates. He was one of several at fault when Hull, having dusted themselves down after conceding from Morgan Rogers early on, went ahead through Mohamed Belloumi’s quickfire double. The ease with which Chelsea’s advantage was handed over left the normally calm and considered Xabi Alonso accusing his side of being “soft” without the ball.

Alonso craves the comfort of a forgettable win. Chelsea have been exhilarating in attack, but they cannot defend. They are conceding two goals per game and the basketball nature of Alonso’s approach has created chaos rather than control. “It’s all entertaining, but I hope that one day you say it was a boring game and we win,” he said. “It will take time. When we get the lead you still need to be competing and not to give the chance so easily for them to come back.

“Especially in the first goal, we can do much better. It was too soft to give them hope because until then we were controlling, we were creating chances, but that changed the mood. We will get better, but it’s having an impact on our performances.”

It is ridiculous that Rogers, Cole Palmer and João Pedro are having to do so much in attack. Chelsea led after seven minutes, surging forward when they left four players forward at a Hull corner. João Pedro’s pass reached Rogers and the £117m signing from Aston Villa drove past Regan Slater before beating Konstantinos Tzolaki at his near post with a low, hard and early shot from the left.

Chelsea should have pushed on after becoming the first side to breach Hull since their promotion. Pedro Neto tested Tzolakis from the right, but the hosts became vague and complacent. This was the first time they have dominated possession in a league game this season and the result was not convincing. Hull limited them to an xG of 0.89, highlighting Chelsea’s issues against low blocks, and were clinical when they attacked.

The soft defending Alonso referenced for the equaliser started with Malo Gusto failing to deal with a long punt from Tzolakis in the 28th minute. Ryan Giles outmuscled the right-back and hooked a cross to the far post. Jorrel Hato misread the Hull left-back’s delivery, leaving Belloumi to rap a shot past Martínez.

Chelsea are without a win against promoted sides in five home games. They do not smell danger, while Alonso’s decision to leave Maxence Lacroix out at centre-back and shift from a back three to a 4-2-3-1 system backfired. Hull had so much space on the flanks. They pushed again and Belloumi’s flick found Lewie Coyle, who ran off Rogers but saw his shot cleared off the line by Levi Colwill.

“The dynamic in terms of conceding, I don’t like it,” Alonso said. “Open play, set-pieces, long balls, this toughness, this competitive sense, we can do better.”

There was no response from Chelsea after Colwill turned Coyle’s shot wide. A corner came in from the left, Martínez flapped and Semi Ajayi’s header hit the bar. The ball came to Belloumi, whose shot flew in thanks to a deflection.

Alonso reacted at half-time, Hato making way for Pep Chavarría at left-back. Reece James drew a save from Tzolakis with a free-kick but Hull carried a threat on the break. They almost extended their lead when Martínez spilled a shot from Slater.

Martínez redeemed himself, blocking the rebound from McBurnie, and Chelsea soon levelled. Palmer, otherwise quiet, surprised Hull with a direct run. The No 10 drove down the left and picked out João Pedro, who lashed a shot into the roof of the net.

Hull refused to lie down. Ajayi, Giles and John Egan were outstanding at the back and the visitors maintained their shape when losing Nobel Mendy after a nasty collision with João Pedro.

Jakirovic made bold substitutions. Alonso threw Danny Welbeck on. Palmer scooped over from 20 yards and Tzolakis thwarted Rogers, but Hull had the best chance. Giles crossed again and Mohamed-Ali Cho shot straight at Martínez from close range.

Hull settled for a point. Jakirovic quashed talk of qualifying for Europe, insisting that survival remains the aim. The Bosnian has everyone pulling in the same direction. Before the start of the season he told his staff he would give them seven days off if Hull took eight points from their first five games. Mission completed with a game to spare.

items.title: 知名PE合伙人斯坦福授课：AI 时代的钱到底流向了哪里？
items.summary:
资深科技投资人、Altimeter Capital合伙人Apoorv Agrawal在斯坦福大学的最新授课中，深度拆解了当前3000亿美元AI生态的“倒三角”利益分配格局，并直言AI应用要想突破当前的盈利瓶颈，进军广告领域将是今年的重大事件。


近期，在斯坦福大学的一场公开课程中，Altimeter
items.text:
资深科技投资人、Altimeter Capital合伙人Apoorv Agrawal在斯坦福大学的最新授课中，深度拆解了当前3000亿美元AI生态的“倒三角”利益分配格局，并直言AI应用要想突破当前的盈利瓶颈，进军广告领域将是今年的重大事件。


近期，在斯坦福大学的一场公开课程中，Altimeter Capital合伙人、斯坦福大学兼职讲师Apoorv Agrawal围绕“AI时代的钱到底流向了哪里”这一市场核心关切，进行了深度拆解。


随着全球科技巨头在AI基础设施上投入天文数字的资本支出（Capex），市场对AI商业化前景的审视正变得愈发严苛。Agrawal指出，这是一个规模巨大的超级周期，正如英伟达CEO黄仁勋所言，当前的数据中心建设是一个包含能源、芯片、电力互连和应用的“五层蛋糕”。


但对于投资者和从业者而言，最核心的拷问在于：“我们在资本支出方面投入了巨资，在建设数据中心方面投入了巨资。那么问题来了：你构建的这些模型，它们真的能创造经济价值吗？”

3000亿美元的“倒三角”：75%的收入流向了半导体


回顾过去25年的互联网、移动互联网和云计算革命，其商业变现模式通常呈金字塔状——底层基础设施利润相对微薄，而顶层的应用端攫取了最丰厚的利润。然而，当前的AI生态呈现出截然相反的形态。


Agrawal在授课中直言，生成式AI生态系统与过去的云计算生态截然不同，它呈现出一个“倒三角形”。对于这一现象的底层逻辑，他引用了硅谷知名投资人马克·安德森的观点进行对比：“正如马克·安德森所说，软件吞噬世界，是因为我可以开发软件并将其分发给数百万人，而运行这些软件的边际成本接近于零，软件企业的毛利率高达80%甚至90%。但人工智能的经济模式并非如此。”


这种差异的根源在于算力成本。“人工智能应用的增量用户并不是免费的，因为你需要消耗大量的GPU资源，拥有人工智能用户的成本要高得多。”Agrawal指出，在过去两年AI行业新增的约3000亿美元收入中，“约75%都直接流向了半导体行业；应用业务虽然增长了十倍以上，但仍然没有产生太大的影响。”


在整个技术栈中，半导体层是目前最赚钱的部分。Agrawal给出了极具冲击力的利润率对比：“数据中心业务的毛利率约为75%，上下浮动几个百分点。而应用层的毛利率，我估计在0%到30%之间……差距相当大，原因就在于半导体层有一位玩家（英伟达）几乎独占鳌头。”


打破“均衡态”的催化剂：巨头自研ASIC与资本支出拐点


针对这种由英伟达主导、底层拿走绝大部分利润的“倒三角”格局会维持多久，市场分歧巨大。Agrawal给出了自己的预判：“我猜它在云端保持当前状态的时间可能会比我预期的要长，大约是十年。我感觉这种情况可能会持续更久，因为要达到稳定均衡状态实在太难了。”


不过，他也为投资者指出了观察这一格局可能被打破的两个核心催化剂：


第一是云巨头（超大规模数据中心运营商）在自研芯片上的突破。“如果某个超大规模数据中心运营商的ASIC项目取得突破——无论是谷歌的TPU、Meta的MTIA，还是亚马逊、微软的项目——都可能成为突破口。如果出现突破性进展，我怀疑这将是该层级最大的重新定价。”


第二是巨头资本支出指引的变化。“另一个催化剂是超大规模数据中心运营商的资本支出指引。我建议在座各位都去听听财报电话会议……如果他们停止对资本支出做出大幅预期，可能意味着当前的均衡状态行不通了。”


此外，算力需求结构的切换也值得高度关注。当前英伟达售出的GPU中约有60%用于训练，40%用于推理。Agrawal认为，“随着时间推移，推理任务的份额会逐渐增加”，但推理任务的工作负载极不稳定，这不仅将考验硬件的利用率，也将重塑中介层（推理中间层）的竞争格局。


AI变现的终极猜想：“我们必须进军广告领域”


在应用端，以ChatGPT为代表的消费级AI正面临海量用户与低效变现的矛盾。Agrawal分享了一组核心数据：ChatGPT拥有约10亿用户（相当于Facebook早期的量级），但“约95%的用户都是免费用户”。


对比当前互联网巨头的单用户收益（ARPU），AI应用的差距显而易见：“Alphabet拥有约40亿用户，每用户每年盈利约100美元；Meta拥有约35亿用户，每用户每年盈利约70美元。而领先的人工智能提供商ChatGPT，每用户每年约带来10美元的收益。”


在排除了纯靠知识型工作订阅模式能撑起万亿估值的可能性后，Agrawal抛出了他对AI商业化模式的终极预判：“第二个问题是：我们如何将每用户每年10美元的收益提升到100美元？我不确定单靠广告和订阅是否可行。答案是，我们得进军广告领域。”


他认为，AI大模型在广告投放上具备得天独厚的优势：“ChatGPT或Claude能够投放的广告具有很多优势：更优惠的价格，因为他们能理解你的意图；非常好的归因分析；更高的信任度。”


尽管市场对“在私人AI对话中插入广告”持悲观或怀疑态度，但Agrawal将其类比为十年前市场看空Facebook移动端广告的论调。“我认为这将是今年另一个重大新闻，这绝对会是一件大事……我乐观地认为我们会找到答案，这将是对现有经济模式的一次重大突破。”

blocks.x: 资深科技投资人、Altimeter Capital合伙人Apoorv Agrawal在斯坦福大学的最新授课中，深度拆解了当前3000亿美元AI生态的“倒三角”利益分配格局，并直言AI应用要想突破当前的盈利瓶颈，进军广告领域将是今年的重大事件。
近期，在斯坦福大学的一场公开课程中，Altimeter Capital合伙人、斯坦福大学兼职讲师Apoorv Agrawal围绕“AI时代的钱到底流向了哪里”这一市场核心关切，进行了深度拆解。
随着全球科技巨头在AI基础设施上投入天文数字的资本支出（Capex），市场对AI商业化前景的审视正变得愈发严苛。Agrawal指出，这是一个规模巨大的超级周期，正如英伟达CEO黄仁勋所言，当前的数据中心建设是一个包含能源、芯片、电力互连和应用的“五层蛋糕”。
但对于投资者和从业者而言，最核心的拷问在于：“我们在资本支出方面投入了巨资，在建设数据中心方面投入了巨资。那么问题来了：你构建的这些模型，它们真的能创造经济价值吗？”
3000亿美元的“倒三角”：75%的收入流向了半导体
回顾过去25年的互联网、移动互联网和云计算革命，其商业变现模式通常呈金字塔状——底层基础设施利润相对微薄，而顶层的应用端攫取了最丰厚的利润。然而，当前的AI生态呈现出截然相反的形态。
Agrawal在授课中直言，生成式AI生态系统与过去的云计算生态截然不同，它呈现出一个“倒三角形”。对于这一现象的底层逻辑，他引用了硅谷知名投资人马克·安德森的观点进行对比：“正如马克·安德森所说，软件吞噬世界，是因为我可以开发软件并将其分发给数百万人，而运行这些软件的边际成本接近于零，软件企业的毛利率高达80%甚至90%。但人工智能的经济模式并非如此。”
这种差异的根源在于算力成本。“人工智能应用的增量用户并不是免费的，因为你需要消耗大量的GPU资源，拥有人工智能用户的成本要高得多。”Agrawal指出，在过去两年AI行业新增的约3000亿美元收入中，“约75%都直接流向了半导体行业；应用业务虽然增长了十倍以上，但仍然没有产生太大的影响。”
在整个技术栈中，半导体层是目前最赚钱的部分。Agrawal给出了极具冲击力的利润率对比：“数据中心业务的毛利率约为75%，上下浮动几个百分点。而应用层的毛利率，我估计在0%到30%之间……差距相当大，原因就在于半导体层有一位玩家（英伟达）几乎独占鳌头。”
打破“均衡态”的催化剂：巨头自研ASIC与资本支出拐点
针对这种由英伟达主导、底层拿走绝大部分利润的“倒三角”格局会维持多久，市场分歧巨大。Agrawal给出了自己的预判：“我猜它在云端保持当前状态的时间可能会比我预期的要长，大约是十年。我感觉这种情况可能会持续更久，因为要达到稳定均衡状态实在太难了。”
不过，他也为投资者指出了观察这一格局可能被打破的两个核心催化剂：
第一是云巨头（超大规模数据中心运营商）在自研芯片上的突破。“如果某个超大规模数据中心运营商的ASIC项目取得突破——无论是谷歌的TPU、Meta的MTIA，还是亚马逊、微软的项目——都可能成为突破口。如果出现突破性进展，我怀疑这将是该层级最大的重新定价。”
第二是巨头资本支出指引的变化。“另一个催化剂是超大规模数据中心运营商的资本支出指引。我建议在座各位都去听听财报电话会议……如果他们停止对资本支出做出大幅预期，可能意味着当前的均衡状态行不通了。”
此外，算力需求结构的切换也值得高度关注。当前英伟达售出的GPU中约有60%用于训练，40%用于推理。Agrawal认为，“随着时间推移，推理任务的份额会逐渐增加”，但推理任务的工作负载极不稳定，这不仅将考验硬件的利用率，也将重塑中介层（推理中间层）的竞争格局。
AI变现的终极猜想：“我们必须进军广告领域”
在应用端，以ChatGPT为代表的消费级AI正面临海量用户与低效变现的矛盾。Agrawal分享了一组核心数据：ChatGPT拥有约10亿用户（相当于Facebook早期的量级），但“约95%的用户都是免费用户”。
对比当前互联网巨头的单用户收益（ARPU），AI应用的差距显而易见：“Alphabet拥有约40亿用户，每用户每年盈利约100美元；Meta拥有约35亿用户，每用户每年盈利约70美元。而领先的人工智能提供商ChatGPT，每用户每年约带来10美元的收益。”
在排除了纯靠知识型工作订阅模式能撑起万亿估值的可能性后，Agrawal抛出了他对AI商业化模式的终极预判：“第二个问题是：我们如何将每用户每年10美元的收益提升到100美元？我不确定单靠广告和订阅是否可行。答案是，我们得进军广告领域。”
他认为，AI大模型在广告投放上具备得天独厚的优势：“ChatGPT或Claude能够投放的广告具有很多优势：更优惠的价格，因为他们能理解你的意图；非常好的归因分析；更高的信任度。”
尽管市场对“在私人AI对话中插入广告”持悲观或怀疑态度，但Agrawal将其类比为十年前市场看空Facebook移动端广告的论调。“我认为这将是今年另一个重大新闻，这绝对会是一件大事……我乐观地认为我们会找到答案，这将是对现有经济模式的一次重大突破。”

地球上大约有 80 亿人口，其中 40 亿人上网。消费者应用的大致经济效益是这样的：Alphabet 拥有约 40 亿用户，每用户每年盈利约 100 美元；Meta 拥有约 35 亿用户，每用户每年盈利约 70 美元。
领先的人工智能提供商 ChatGPT 拥有约 10 亿用户，每用户每年约带来 10 美元的收益。所以问题是：我们如何将用户数量从 10 亿提升到 40 亿？知识型工作或许是答案，但我认为我们需要超越知识型工作本身。第二个问题是：我们如何将每用户每年 10 美元的收益提升到 100 美元？我不确定单靠广告和订阅是否可行。
答案是，我们得进军广告领域。而且 ChatGPT 或 Claude 能够投放的广告具有很多优势：更优惠的价格，因为他们能理解你的意图；非常好的归因分析；更高的信任度。我认为这将是今年另一个重大新闻，这绝对会是一件大事。
真正透彻理解广告模式至关重要。十年前 Facebook 上市时，有很多做空 Facebook 的报告，因为人们说："这些广告在电脑上效果不错，但在手机上肯定不行，因为手机空间不够。"令人惊讶的是，我们最终还是在手机上找到了空间。
现在的情况也一样——"我正在进行这场非常私人的对话，我不想被广告打断"，这就是看空的论据。我无法预测最终结果，但我乐观地认为我们会找到答案，这将是对现有经济模式的一次重大突破。我们会在今年晚些时候的某个演讲环节深入探讨这个问题。
谢谢大家。

items.title: 高盛对冲基金主管：“零日期权”压制美股波动，科技和能源仍是最佳选择
items.summary:
美股正处于一场多空拉锯之中，而一股来自期权市场的隐性力量正将标普500指数的日内波动锁定在异常狭窄的区间内。


高盛对冲基金业务主管Tony
items.text:
美股正处于一场多空拉锯之中，而一股来自期权市场的隐性力量正将标普500指数的日内波动锁定在异常狭窄的区间内。


高盛对冲基金业务主管Tony Pasquariello在最新市场宏观报告中警告称，"当前的交易并不容易"。他指出，股市一方面受到油价上涨和利率走高的压制，另一方面又获得企业盈利增长的支撑，整体陷入僵局。与此同时，高盛经济学家David Mericle已将9月美联储议息会议加息25个基点纳入预测，尽管他本人认为当前经济形势并不构成加息的强有力理由。


在市场结构层面，高盛衍生品策略师Brian Garrett指出，以"零日到期期权"（0-DTE）为代表的波动率收割策略规模庞大，在缺乏日内催化剂的情况下，这类策略会将市场强制压缩在更窄的波动区间内。尽管宏观不确定性高企，Pasquariello仍维持对能源和科技板块的双重看多立场，并将美国财政可持续性列为美股最大的长期风险。


零日期权制造“27天紧身衣”


令Pasquariello感到意外的是，过去27个交易日内，标普500指数的日内交易区间始终低于1%——这是新冠疫情暴发以来持续时间最长的低波动纪录。

对此，Brian Garrett给出了结构性解释："这反映了当前的市场结构。交易量偏低、重要消息相对匮乏，使得期权市场在日内交易中扮演了更重要的角色。0-DTE的'收益'策略在标普期权市场规模巨大，这类策略从早上9点30分开市便开始运作，在缺乏日内催化剂的情况下，会将市场强制压入更窄的波动区间。"


Pasquariello将这一现象概括为：零日期权可以在一定程度上"拴住"日内波动区间，但这种压制并非无限期有效。一旦重大催化剂出现，被压缩的波动能量将集中释放。


美联储加息预期升温，但经济基本面存疑


在宏观层面，高盛首席经济学家David Mericle已将9月美联储会议加息25个基点纳入预测基准情景，但他同时明确表示，这一加息决定缺乏强有力的经济依据。


Mericle认为，通胀超出2%目标的部分可归因于一次性因素，其影响预计将逐步消退；过去三个月核心PCE通胀率降至约2.5%的水平，是上述判断的早期信号。他还指出，通胀看似广泛蔓延，主要源于关税效应，而非经济过热，通胀预期目前也未面临脱锚的迫切风险。


高盛美国投资组合策略团队负责人Ben Snider则梳理了过去七轮加息周期中美股的历史表现：加息启动后的前三个月，标普500平均下跌2%；但此后12个月平均反弹9%。唯一的重大例外是2022年的大幅调整。Snider的研究还显示，在加息初期表现最佳的两个板块正是科技和能源。


科技与能源：高盛不愿放弃的核心配对


Pasquariello在报告中强调，2026年是极为特殊的一年，每周都像是一场独立的冒险，动量因子经历了一系列剧烈波动。但在这一切之中，做多能源（年内涨幅+44%）与做多科技（年内涨幅+23%）的组合持续创造回报。

在科技前景方面，高盛另一位分析师Rich Privorotsky援引业界一线人士的判断称："那些处于技术最前沿的人告诉你，技术进步的速度快得令人震惊，以至于他们需要主动放慢节奏。这本身就是对这项技术的巨大背书。安全和对齐问题确实存在，解决好这些问题至关重要——'这东西真的有效'的信息，已经内嵌在这一警告之中。"


Pasquariello表示，考虑到当前宏观动态，他不倾向于放弃能源加科技、以及全球利率多头与股票多头这两组配对策略。


仓位偏防御，市场情绪降至年内低点


从持仓数据来看，高盛主经纪商账簿显示，当前净敞口处于过去一年的第26百分位，上周宏观产品的净卖出规模更是创下"解放日"以来最大单周降幅。


高盛美国投资组合策略的情绪指标目前读数为-0.5个标准差，为今年3月以来最低，处于过去十年的第26百分位。


Pasquariello表示，他理解主动管理型投资者为何选择在季节性表现历来较弱的时期削减风险敞口，也清楚系统性基金在价格下行时可能被迫进一步减仓。但他仍预期市场将在9月和10月完成必要的调整，并为年末两个月的行情奠定良好的技术面基础。


财政可持续性是美股最大长期风险


Pasquariello在报告中将美国财政可持续性列为美股最大的长期风险，并直言这一问题最终可能导致大幅加税或利率长期高企，两种结果对股票投资者而言均非利好。


他同时注意到，彭博大宗商品指数（BCOM）尽管面临季节性不利因素，近期已强势突破2022年高点，这一信号值得关注。


在Pasquariello看来，当前市场是一条"蓄势待发、仓位偏轻的走势，正走向一个被市场用一个月时间拒绝定价的催化剂周"。零日期权可以暂时压制日内波动，但这种压制终有极限。

items.title: 键合设备革命性周期：HBM大扩产，混合键合技术平台化打开第二增长曲线！
